rows.name: Berlin-Dahlem
rows.blurb: Where Hahn and Strassmann found barium and fission was discovered.
rows.fact: At the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found barium after bombarding uranium with neutrons in December 1938. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch then explained it.

rows.name: Calder Hall, Sellafield
rows.blurb: Opened in 1956 and called the first commercial nuclear power station.
rows.fact: Queen Elizabeth II formally opened Calder Hall on 17 October 1956. The UK government calls it the world's first commercial nuclear power station, and it helped establish the UK's civil nuclear industry.

rows.name: CERN
rows.blurb: The particle physics laboratory astride the French-Swiss border.
rows.fact: Founded in 1954, CERN sits astride the Franco-Swiss border near Geneva. Its scientists study fundamental particles with accelerators such as the Large Hadron Collider, the world's largest and most powerful.

rows.name: Chernobyl
rows.blurb: The 1986 reactor accident that reshaped nuclear safety worldwide.
rows.fact: On 26 April 1986 a turbine test at reactor 4 ended in a steam explosion that destroyed the reactor and released radioactive material. The cause was a flawed design plus serious operator mistakes.

rows.name: Chicago Pile-1
rows.blurb: The first reactor to reach a self-sustaining chain reaction.
rows.fact: On 2 December 1942 a team led by Enrico Fermi started the first self-sustaining fission chain reaction, in a former squash court under the stands of the University of Chicago's Stagg Field.

rows.name: Fukushima Daiichi
rows.blurb: A plant hit by an earthquake and tsunami in March 2011.
rows.fact: After the 9.0 earthquake on 11 March 2011, a tsunami flooded the plant and disabled most of its backup generators and the heat exchangers that carry reactor and decay heat to the sea. The three reactors lost proper cooling and water circulation.

rows.name: Hanford
rows.blurb: Home of the world's first production reactors, on the Columbia River.
rows.fact: Workers at Hanford, along the Columbia River in Washington state, built and ran the world's first nuclear production reactors, which made plutonium for the Manhattan Project.

rows.name: Hiroshima
rows.blurb: Bombed on 6 August 1945, now a city of remembrance and peace.
rows.fact: An atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945. The city was rebuilt under the 1949 Hiroshima Peace Memorial City Construction Law, and its Peace Memorial Museum shares the message "No More Hiroshimas".

rows.name: ITER
rows.blurb: A giant fusion experiment being built in southern France.
rows.fact: ITER is building the world's largest tokamak in southern France. Its goal is fusion power at power-plant scale, with China, the EU, India, Japan, Korea, Russia and the United States taking part.

rows.name: Los Alamos
rows.blurb: The secret wartime laboratory of the Manhattan Project.
rows.fact: Manhattan Project administrators found an ideal location in Los Alamos, New Mexico, for a secret laboratory. Scientists such as J. Robert Oppenheimer, Hans Bethe and Richard Feynman worked there during the Manhattan Project.

rows.name: Manchester
rows.blurb: Where Rutherford showed the atom has a tiny, dense centre.
rows.fact: Geiger and Marsden's alpha-particle experiments in Rutherford's lab led him to conclude in 1911 that most of an atom's mass and charge sit in a very small central body, later called the nucleus.

rows.name: Nagasaki
rows.blurb: Bombed on 9 August 1945, and a voice for peace ever since.
rows.fact: At 11:02 a.m. on 9 August 1945 the explosion of an atomic bomb devastated Nagasaki. The city's Atomic Bomb Museum says the experience must be passed on to future generations.

rows.name: Oak Ridge
rows.blurb: The secret town that enriched uranium during the Manhattan Project.
rows.fact: The top-secret program at Oak Ridge began in 1942. Its facilities produced enriched uranium, and the town served as headquarters of the Manhattan Project after it moved from New York City.

rows.name: Obninsk
rows.blurb: Home of an early nuclear power plant that made electricity in 1954.
rows.fact: The 5 MWe Obninsk reactor was Russia's first nuclear power plant. In 1954 it was the first in the world to produce electricity.

rows.name: Oklo
rows.blurb: Natural nuclear reactors that ran about two billion years ago.
rows.fact: In a uranium deposit in what is now Gabon, fission began about two billion years ago. Natural water served as a moderator, there was no neutron-absorbing material such as cadmium or lead, and the chain reaction sustained itself.

rows.name: Paris, the Curies' shed
rows.blurb: Where Marie and Pierre Curie announced polonium and radium.
rows.fact: In July 1898 the Curies announced polonium, named after Marie's homeland, and in December they reported radium. They worked in an old shed across the courtyard of their school, once a dissecting room.

rows.name: Three Mile Island
rows.blurb: A partial meltdown in 1979 that changed how plants are run and checked.
rows.fact: On 28 March 1979 a stuck-open valve and misread instruments led to a partial meltdown of Unit 2. Small releases had no detectable health effects, and the accident brought wide changes in training and oversight.

rows.name: Trinity Site
rows.blurb: The desert site of the first nuclear test, 16 July 1945.
rows.fact: At 5:30 am on 16 July 1945, the world's first nuclear test device was detonated at the Alamogordo Gun Range. The test exposed nearby and downwind residents to radiation with long-lasting effects.
